front: Outline how urbanisation alters the water cycle in a drainage basin. (4 marks)
back:
Model answer: Concrete and tarmac are impermeable, so infiltration falls (1) and overland flow rises (d). Drains carry water quickly to channels (1), shortening lag time and raising peak discharge (d). Less vegetation means less interception and transpiration (1).
Marking points: Point marked, AO1 only. 1 mark per valid change, (d) for developing it. Max 3 if only one factor. Max 1 for a list of factors with no development.
Common trap: Writing about flood damage to people instead of changes to stores and flows, or listing factors with no development.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Explain the concept of positive feedback in the carbon cycle. (4 marks)
back:
Model answer: Positive feedback amplifies an initial change (1). Warming thaws permafrost (1), which releases stored carbon as CO2 and methane (d). This adds to the greenhouse effect, causing more warming and more thaw (d).
Marking points: Point marked, AO1. 1 for an accurate definition, then marks for an example developed as a linked loop.
Common trap: Describing negative feedback (which dampens change), or giving a definition with no example of the loop.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Outline the processes that transfer carbon from the atmosphere into the ocean store. (4 marks)
back:
Model answer: CO2 dissolves into surface seawater (1), more readily in cold water (d). Phytoplankton take in CO2 by photosynthesis (1). When they die, carbon sinks to the deep ocean and sea-floor sediments, the biological pump (d).
Marking points: Point marked, AO1. Credit each named process plus development. Max 3 if only one process.
Common trap: Drifting away from the key term, here writing about acidification effects on coral instead of transfer processes. Off-term points score nothing.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: A drainage basin has annual precipitation of 900 mm, evapotranspiration of 450 mm and runoff of 380 mm. Calculate the change in storage and state what it shows.
back:
Model answer: Water balance P = Q + E +/- change in storage. 900 - 450 - 380 = +70 mm. Storage increased by 70 mm, so the basin has a water surplus that year.
Marking points: Correct equation, correct working, units (mm), and a correct comment on surplus or deficit.
Common trap: Subtracting in the wrong order or dropping the sign, so a surplus is called a deficit.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Figure shows monthly precipitation (bars) and mean river discharge (line) for a UK drainage basin over one year. Analyse the data shown. (6 marks)
back:
Model answer: Overall, discharge is highest in winter, when precipitation is also highest, so the two are positively linked. Quote the peak months and values, and calculate a difference or ratio between the wettest and driest months. Note any anomaly, such as a wet summer month with little rise in discharge.
Marking points: AO3 only. Level 2 (4-6): clear analysis, appropriate use of data, clear connections between the data sets. Level 1: basic, little data.
Common trap: Explaining why, such as summer evapotranspiration. Explanation is AO2 and gains no credit here.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Using a figure showing land-use change in a river catchment and your own knowledge, assess how the changes affect flood risk. (6 marks)
back:
Model answer: The figure shows woodland replaced by housing and arable fields near the river. Less interception and infiltration plus drains mean faster runoff, a shorter lag time and a higher peak. Urban land beside the channel matters most, as it is close and impermeable. Judgement: flood risk rises, most in the lower catchment.
Marking points: AO1 2, AO2 4. Level 2 needs knowledge applied clearly to the resource and a judgement. No specific place knowledge needed.
Common trap: Only re-describing the figure (AO3), or reciting flood knowledge with no link to the figure (AO1 only).
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Assess the extent to which wildfires disrupt the carbon cycle. (9 marks)
back:
Model answer: Combustion moves carbon from biomass to the atmosphere in hours. In fire-adapted ecosystems regrowth re-absorbs it over years to decades. Peat and soil fires release long-term stores that are slow to recover. Warming brings more frequent fires, a positive feedback. Judgement: disruption is short term unless fires burn peat or become more frequent.
Marking points: AO1 4, AO2 5. This links Hazards to Water and carbon. Level 3 needs detailed carbon knowledge.
Common trap: Narrating a fire event without carbon stores, flows and timescales.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: With reference to a tropical rainforest you have studied, assess the extent to which human activity has changed its water and carbon cycles. (20 marks)
back:
Model answer: Intro: in the Amazon, deforestation is the main driver. Carbon: burning shifts carbon from biomass and soil to the atmosphere. Water: less transpiration and recycled rainfall, more runoff. Link the cycles: a drier forest burns more, a positive feedback. Counterweight: natural droughts and reforestation (Brazil's target: 12 million hectares by 2030). Conclusion.
Marking points: AO1 10, AO2 10. Level 4: case study detail throughout, scale and time, a firm conclusion.
Common trap: Ignoring natural factors, or describing the forest without saying how much the cycles changed.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Assess the effectiveness of human interventions designed to reduce carbon transfers to the atmosphere. (20 marks)
back:
Model answer: Set a position, then judge each intervention by scale, speed, cost and politics. Afforestation is cheap but slow to store carbon. Carbon capture and storage works only at a small scale so far. Renewable energy cuts emissions at the source. Global agreements such as Paris 2015 depend on nations keeping their pledges. Conclusion: decide which works best and why.
Marking points: AO1 10, AO2 10. Level 3 and 4 need evaluation and a supported conclusion. Recall alone caps at Level 2.
Common trap: Listing strategies without judging them, or drifting into the causes of climate change.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Outline the processes leading to the formation of a spit. (4 marks)
back:
Model answer: Longshore drift moves sediment along the coast in the direction of the prevailing wind (1). Where the coastline changes direction, sediment is deposited into open water (1) and builds a ridge (d). Wave refraction and changing winds curve the end into a hook (1). Saltmarsh forms in the sheltered water behind (d).
Marking points: Point marked, AO1. A logical sequence of processes earns the marks. Max 3 if only one process.
Common trap: Describing what the spit looks like instead of the processes that formed it.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Outline the characteristics of a wave-cut platform. (4 marks)
back:
Model answer: A gently sloping rocky surface at the foot of a cliff (1), extending out to sea (d). It is covered at high tide and exposed at low tide (1). The surface is uneven, with rock pools and ridges along weaker joints (1). A notch or cliff line marks its landward edge (d).
Marking points: Point marked, AO1. Credit features that make the landform distinct. Formation is credited only where it overlaps with characteristics.
Common trap: Writing about how it formed instead of its characteristics.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Figure shows cliff erosion rates (m per year) at survey points along a coastline, with a geology map. Analyse the data shown. (6 marks)
back:
Model answer: Overall, erosion is fastest on the clay sections and slowest on the chalk headland. Quote the highest and lowest rates and how many times faster one is. Use the scale and direction: rates increase towards the south. Point out anomalies, such as a fast-eroding clay site next to slow ones. Connect the rates to the geology map.
Marking points: AO3 only. Level 2: clear analysis, accurate data use and clear connections between figures. Level 1: basic.
Common trap: Explaining why clay erodes fast (AO2, no credit), or treating the two figures separately with no link.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Pebble lengths (cm) at 6 sites on a beach are 3, 5, 6, 6, 7, 9. Calculate the standard deviation and evaluate how useful it is for this data. (6 marks)
back:
Model answer: Mean = 36 / 6 = 6. Squared deviations: 9, 1, 0, 0, 1, 9 = 20. 20 / 6 = 3.33, and the square root is 1.83 cm. 4 of 6 values (67%) lie within 1 SD (4.17-7.83 cm). The SD shows the spread around the mean, but it is more useful when compared with another beach, and n = 6 is small.
Marking points: AO3. Marks for an accurate table and the final calculation (method credit even if the answer is wrong), then up to 3 for evaluation points.
Common trap: Doing the calculation but never evaluating how useful the technique is.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Using only two maps of the same coastline from different dates, evaluate their relative usefulness in showing coastal change. (6 marks)
back:
Model answer: Map A has a scale and grid, so change can be measured, but its key differs from Map B's, which makes comparison harder. The time gap between the maps is long, so the rate of change is hidden. Neither map shows height, so cliff retreat cannot be judged. Overall, Map A is more useful.
Marking points: AO3. Evaluate the presentation: scale, keys, dates, accuracy and missing information. Reach a judgement on relative usefulness.
Common trap: Analysing the change shown instead of judging the sources, which earns little credit.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Using a figure showing a proposed managed realignment scheme and your own knowledge, assess the sustainability of this approach. (6 marks)
back:
Model answer: The figure shows an embankment breached to flood farmland and create saltmarsh. Saltmarsh absorbs wave energy, adds habitat and stores carbon. Long-term costs are lower than maintaining walls. Against this, farmland is lost and landowners need compensation. Judgement: sustainable if the community supports it.
Marking points: AO1 2, AO2 4. Level 2 needs knowledge applied to the resource and a judgement. No case study recital is needed.
Common trap: Reciting a learned case study, or only basic hard v soft engineering, instead of engaging with the figure.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Assess the relative importance of geology in the development of landforms on high-energy erosional coastlines. (20 marks)
back:
Model answer: Position: geology sets the template; marine energy drives change. Rock type and structure matter, such as concordant and discordant coasts in Dorset. Joints guide caves, arches and stacks, as at Old Harry. Also weigh fetch, destructive waves, sub-aerial processes and sea level change. Conclusion: rank the factors.
Marking points: AO1 10, AO2 10. Level 4 needs detailed processes, named examples and a judgement on relative importance.
Common trap: Drifting into coastal management, which is relevant only through knock-on effects such as starving downdrift beaches of sediment.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: With reference to a coastal landscape beyond the UK, evaluate human responses to the risks it presents. (20 marks)
back:
Model answer: Name the coast, such as the Sundarbans in Bangladesh, and its risks: cyclones, storm surge and sea level rise. Evaluate each response: mangrove protection, embankments, cyclone shelters and early warnings. Compare resilience, mitigation and adaptation over time. Conclusion: decide which responses work and for whom.
Marking points: AO1 10, AO2 10. Level 4 needs a detailed case study and an evaluative conclusion based on the evidence.
Common trap: Using a UK case study, or narrating the area's problems without evaluating the responses.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Assess the impact of sea level change on the development of coastal landscapes. (20 marks)
back:
Model answer: Separate eustatic, isostatic and tectonic change. Emergence leaves raised beaches and marine platforms. Submergence creates rias, fjords and Dalmatian coasts. Sea level rise moves erosion and deposition inland, threatening spits and saltmarsh. Weigh this against waves, geology and human management. Conclusion: judge how far it shapes landscapes compared with other factors.
Marking points: AO1 10, AO2 10. Level 4 needs links from process to landform and an awareness of time.
Common trap: Describing the impacts of sea level rise on people and barely reaching the landforms.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Outline the processes involved in the formation of a deep-sea trench. (4 marks)
back:
Model answer: At a destructive margin, oceanic crust meets another plate (1). The denser oceanic plate is subducted (1), pulled down by slab pull (d). The downward flexing plate forms a long, deep trench parallel to the margin (d).
Marking points: Point marked, AO1. Credit a correct sequence starting from convergence and subduction.
Common trap: Confusing trenches with ocean ridges (constructive margins), which earns almost no credit.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Outline the Park model of human response to hazards. (4 marks)
back:
Model answer: A graph of quality of life against time, before and after a hazard event (1). Quality of life drops sharply during the event and the relief phase (1). It recovers through rehabilitation and reconstruction (d). The depth of the fall and the level of recovery depend on preparedness and development (d).
Marking points: Point marked, AO1. Credit the axes, the phases and what controls the curve's shape.
Common trap: Describing the Hazard Management Cycle instead, or narrating one event without the model.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Figure is a scatter graph of earthquake magnitude against deaths, with deaths on a logarithmic scale and countries labelled. Analyse the data shown. (6 marks)
back:
Model answer: Overall there is only a weak positive relationship between magnitude and deaths. Read the log axis correctly: each gridline is 10 times the one below. Quote the extremes and the difference between them. Name anomalies, such as a high-magnitude event with few deaths. Group the labelled countries if a pattern appears.
Marking points: AO3 only. Level 2: clear analysis, accurate data use and clear connections.
Common trap: Misreading the logarithmic scale, or explaining the anomalies by development level, which is AO2 and gets no credit.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Assess the usefulness of a map of one season's tropical storm tracks, coloured by intensity, in showing the hazard risk to coastal populations. (6 marks)
back:
Model answer: The map is useful because it shows where storms tracked and how intense they were, so exposed coasts stand out. Its limits: it covers one season only, shows no population or vulnerability, and gives no storm surge or rainfall data. Overall it is of limited use for judging risk to people.
Marking points: AO3. Evaluate what the resource shows and what it omits, and reach a judgement.
Common trap: Analysing the storm tracks instead of evaluating the resource. Careful evaluation often shows a resource is less useful than it first seems.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Using a figure showing a volcano, its hazard zones, valleys and nearby settlements, and your own knowledge, assess the challenges of managing volcanic hazards in this area. (9 marks)
back:
Model answer: Settlements lie in valleys that lahars would follow, so hazard zoning is vital but hard to enforce. Monitoring (tiltmeters, gas, seismometers) gives warning, but few roads slow evacuation. Remoteness stretches emergency services. Ash threatens farms and livelihoods. Judgement: name the biggest challenge.
Marking points: AO1 4, AO2 5. Level 3 needs detailed knowledge applied to the resource and a balanced, coherent argument.
Common trap: Analysing the figure instead of thinking as a manager about the challenges.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: To what extent is prediction more important than preparedness in reducing the impacts of tropical storms? (9 marks)
back:
Model answer: Satellite tracking gives days of warning, so prediction is the starting point. Warnings save lives only when people can act on them through shelters, evacuation plans and transport. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 was well forecast, but many residents without cars stayed. Judgement: prediction is necessary but preparedness decides the outcome.
Marking points: AO1 4, AO2 5. Level 3 needs a clear view on the extent, supported by examples.
Common trap: Contrasting two storms in detail without answering the "to what extent" question.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Assess the role of international organisations in reducing the impacts of tectonic hazards. (9 marks)
back:
Model answer: The UN's Sendai Framework of 2015 sets disaster-risk targets, and the Red Cross and World Bank fund relief and rebuilding. After the 2010 Haiti earthquake, aid was large but poorly coordinated. Building codes and national planning, as in Japan, often matter more. Judgement: international help is valuable but secondary to national action.
Marking points: AO1 4, AO2 5. This links Hazards to Global governance. Level 3 needs named organisations and an assessment.
Common trap: A generic account of "aid" with no named organisation and no judgement.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: 'Level of development is the most important factor in determining the impact of earthquakes.' To what extent do you agree? (20 marks)
back:
Model answer: Position: development matters, but physical factors and governance also count. Haiti 2010 (magnitude 7.0) shows how poverty and weak buildings raise deaths. In Tohoku 2011, a rich country still suffered huge losses from the tsunami. In Turkey-Syria 2023, poorly enforced building codes mattered. Also weigh depth, distance and secondary hazards. Conclusion: a clear, ranked judgement.
Marking points: AO1 10, AO2 10. Level 4 needs detailed case studies used to argue throughout.
Common trap: Comparing two case studies in sequence without a sustained argument about "most important".
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: Assess the extent to which human responses enable the continued occupation of a multi-hazardous environment you have studied. (20 marks)
back:
Model answer: In the Philippines, the hazards are typhoons, earthquakes and volcanoes, on a plate boundary in a storm belt. Responses include PAGASA forecasts, PHIVOLCS monitoring, evacuation before Pinatubo in 1991 and rebuilding after Typhoon Haiyan in 2013. Weigh resilience and adaptation against poverty and rising risk. Conclusion: occupation continues, but at what cost.
Marking points: AO1 10, AO2 10. Level 4 needs physical and human factors and a firm judgement.
Common trap: Not grasping "human occupation", or ignoring the physical setting.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 1: Physical geography

front: In a Changing places 4-mark question on your place study, how much credit does simply naming a data source earn?
back: None. You must say how you used it and what it showed about the place.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: In the AQA 6-mark "Using Figure X and your own knowledge" question, what must a Level 2 answer include?
back: Clear reference to the figure, as well as your own knowledge
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: Outline the role of the WTO in regulating global trade. (4 marks)
back:
Model answer: The WTO sets the rules for trade between its members (1). It hosts negotiations to cut tariffs and other barriers (1). Its dispute settlement system rules on complaints between members (1) and can authorise retaliatory tariffs (d).
Marking points: Point marked, AO1. No mark for just naming the institution. Points must refer to its role in regulating.
Common trap: Mixing up the roles of the WTO, IMF and World Bank, which earns only 1 mark.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: Outline the threats to Antarctica from tourism. (4 marks)
back:
Model answer: Visitors are concentrated on the Antarctic Peninsula in a short summer (1). Trampling damages fragile mosses and lichens (1), and landings disturb penguin colonies (d). Alien species arrive on clothing and boots (1). Ship groundings risk fuel spills (d).
Marking points: Point marked, AO1. Each threat must state its impact.
Common trap: Vague threats with no impact stated, such as "tourism harms wildlife", which are not creditworthy.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: Outline what is meant by the 'global commons'. (4 marks)
back:
Model answer: Areas and resources outside any one nation's jurisdiction (1), shared by all, such as the high seas, atmosphere and Antarctica (1). Hardin's 'tragedy of the commons' describes overuse when nobody owns them (d). Protecting them therefore needs international governance (d).
Marking points: Point marked, AO1. A definition, then development through the concept and its management.
Common trap: Giving only a list of examples with no definition, which earns max 1.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: Figure shows a TNC's annual revenue (compound bar graph by product) and a world map of its offices (proportional symbols). Analyse the data shown. (6 marks)
back:
Model answer: Overview: revenue rises every year. Read the scale accurately and give the overall rise and a percentage. Say which product's share grows. On the map, offices cluster in a few regions, with others nearly absent. Name an anomaly. Connect the two: the largest office regions match the growing products' markets if the data shows it.
Marking points: AO3. Level 2: big picture, accurate data, manipulation, anomalies and connections between figures.
Common trap: Treating each figure separately, or explaining the growth through globalisation (no credit).
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: Using a figure showing how the retail price of a cup of coffee is shared between farmers, exporters, roasters and retailers, and your own knowledge, assess how fair world trade in this commodity is. (6 marks)
back:
Model answer: The figure shows farmers receive a small share and retailers in consuming countries the most. Value is added after export, so producer countries gain little. Tariff escalation and TNC buying power keep farm prices low. Fairtrade raises returns only for a small share of farmers. Judgement: the trade is unequal.
Marking points: AO1 2, AO2 4. Level 2 must use the figure and add own knowledge.
Common trap: Reciting a learned commodity case study without using the figure.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: 'Global governance has protected Antarctica successfully as a global common.' To what extent do you agree? (20 marks)
back:
Model answer: Position: success on mining, weaker on fishing and climate. The Antarctic Treaty (1959) froze territorial claims. The Madrid Protocol (1991) bans mineral activity. CCAMLR sets fishing limits, but illegal toothfish fishing continues. The IWC moratorium (1982) still saw Japanese whaling there until 2019. Climate change lies beyond the Treaty's control. Conclusion.
Marking points: AO1 10, AO2 10. Level 4 needs a critical view of named agreements and threats.
Common trap: Covering climate change only, or factual errors such as polar bears in Antarctica.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: With reference to a TNC you have studied, assess the extent to which its impacts on the countries where it operates are positive. (20 marks)
back:
Model answer: Name the TNC, such as Apple: designed in the USA, assembled by contractors such as Foxconn in China. Positives: jobs, skills and export earnings. Negatives: worker conditions and tax issues, such as the EU ruling that Ireland recover 13 billion euros. Weigh up the host countries in turn. Conclusion: a judgement on the extent.
Marking points: AO1 10, AO2 10. Level 4 needs specific TNC detail and a sustained argument.
Common trap: A stark "producers lose, consumers win" contrast, or a generic TNC with no named company.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: 'Globalisation has created more inequality than it has reduced.' Critically assess this statement. (20 marks)
back:
Model answer: Position. Benefits: China's growth lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty. Costs: wider gaps within countries, labour exploitation such as the Rana Plaza collapse in 2013, and environmental damage. Weigh by scale (between v within countries) and time. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement.
Marking points: AO1 10, AO2 10. Level 4 needs a sustained line of reasoning with integrated examples.
Common trap: Dropping in a learned case study (bananas, Apple) whether it fits or not, giving a directionless answer.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: Outline the difference between insider and outsider perspectives on place. (4 marks)
back:
Model answer: An insider feels at home and belongs to a place (1). An outsider feels unfamiliar or excluded, such as a tourist or recent migrant (1). The same place can hold different meanings for the two, such as a resort for residents and visitors (d). A person can move from outsider to insider over time (d).
Marking points: Point marked, AO1. Definitions earn 2. Full marks need the difference to be developed.
Common trap: Stopping at two definitions, or naming a place without developing it.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: Outline how you used one quantitative data source to investigate economic change in your distant place study. (4 marks)
back:
Model answer: Name the place and the source, such as census employment by industry for two dates (1). It showed manufacturing's share falling and services rising (1)(d). This linked to deindustrialisation and how residents' work changed (d).
Marking points: Point marked, AO1. No mark for only naming the source. Max 3 if the place is not identified. Link the source to the place and the theme.
Common trap: Evaluating the reliability of the source, which is not asked, or describing the source without saying how it was used.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: Outline how exogenous factors contribute to the character of a place. (4 marks)
back:
Model answer: Exogenous factors are a place's relationships with other places (1). Migration brings cultural diversity, such as the Bangladeshi community shaping Brick Lane (d). Flows of investment and TNC decisions change local jobs and land use (1). Transport links tie a place into regional and global networks (d).
Marking points: Point marked, AO1. Correct concept, then developed examples.
Common trap: Writing about endogenous factors (location, topography), which earn no credit here.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: Figure is a triangular graph showing the percentage of residents aged 0-15, 16-64 and 65+ in each ward of a city. Analyse the data shown. (6 marks)
back:
Model answer: Read each point on all three axes; they add up to 100%. Overall, most wards cluster at 60-70% aged 16-64. Contrast the ward with the most residents aged 65+ with the most youthful ward, quoting values. Name outliers and any grouping of wards.
Marking points: AO3. Level 2: accurate reading, data in support, anomalies and connections.
Common trap: Not knowing how to read a triangular graph and describing the whole city instead of individual wards.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: Evaluate the usefulness of an old photograph and a census table in showing how a place has changed. (6 marks)
back:
Model answer: The photograph shows the built environment and the feel of the street, but it captures one moment chosen by the photographer. The census is quantitative and comparable over time, but it comes only every 10 years and boundaries change. Together they complement each other. Judgement: say which is more useful for this change.
Marking points: AO3. Credit strengths, limitations and a judgement on each source.
Common trap: Analysing the change shown instead of judging how useful the sources are.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: Using a figure showing a tourist brochure image of a regenerated waterfront and your own knowledge, assess how external agencies try to change the meaning of this place. (6 marks)
back:
Model answer: The brochure shows a selective image of heritage and leisure that hides the area's industrial past. Councils and developers rebrand places to attract visitors and investment, as at Liverpool's Albert Dock. Insiders can feel excluded as prices rise. Judgement: the image changes outsiders' meaning more than residents'.
Marking points: AO1 2, AO2 4. Level 2 needs the figure used with own knowledge.
Common trap: Writing about "a place" in general, or about other examples only, instead of the place in the figure.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: With reference to your distant place study, assess the extent to which people's lived experience there has changed over time. (20 marks)
back:
Model answer: Name the place, such as Detroit or Shoreditch. Describe past lived experience using sources such as oral histories and photographs. Explain the change driven by deindustrialisation, migration and investment. Note what has stayed the same, and how groups differ, such as long-term residents v newcomers. Conclusion: a judgement on the extent.
Marking points: AO1 10, AO2 10. Level 4 needs accurate, detailed place knowledge with scale and time integrated.
Common trap: Writing about both local and distant places when the question asks for one, or using outdated stereotypes.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: 'Flows of people shape the character of places more than flows of money and investment.' To what extent do you agree? (20 marks)
back:
Model answer: Position. People: migration made Newham one of the UK's most diverse boroughs. Money: Olympic investment transformed Stratford, while the loss of car-industry investment emptied Detroit. The two interact, as investment attracts people. Conclusion: a judgement backed by the places.
Marking points: AO1 10, AO2 10. Level 4 needs a clear line of reasoning with an accurate timeline.
Common trap: Timeline errors, such as treating Albert Dock regeneration as a cause of deindustrialisation, or case study recital.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: Outline the reasons for urban resurgence. (4 marks)
back:
Model answer: Urban resurgence is people and businesses returning to city centres (1). Regeneration policies reused brownfield land (1), creating flats and offices (d). Growth of service and knowledge jobs draws young professionals (1), and students also move in (d).
Marking points: Point marked, AO1. Define the term, then give developed reasons.
Common trap: Treating resurgence as the same thing as regeneration or gentrification, with no link to population returning.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: Outline how urban areas affect wind. (4 marks)
back:
Model answer: Buildings add friction, so average wind speeds are lower than in rural areas (1). Streets between tall buildings channel wind (1), increasing its speed in a canyon effect (d). Tall buildings deflect wind downwards, creating gusts and eddies at street level (d).
Marking points: Point marked, AO1. Credit each effect plus development.
Common trap: Writing about the urban heat island or pollution instead of wind.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: Figure shows storm hydrographs for an urban and a rural catchment after the same rainfall event. Analyse the data shown. (6 marks)
back:
Model answer: The urban peak is higher and earlier. Quote both peaks, the ratio between them, and the difference in lag time in hours. The urban rising limb is steeper and its discharge falls back faster. Both start from a similar base flow. Note any anomaly.
Marking points: AO3. Level 2: clear analysis with data, manipulation and comparison.
Common trap: Explaining the difference with impermeable surfaces (AO2, no credit), or misreading the time axis.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: Using a photograph and map of a cultural quarter and your own knowledge, to what extent do cultural and heritage quarters benefit all urban residents? (9 marks)
back:
Model answer: The figures show reused old buildings with galleries and cafes. Benefits: jobs, tourism and the reuse of derelict heritage. Costs: rising rents and gentrification push out low-income residents. Judgement: benefits go mainly to newcomers and businesses.
Marking points: AO1 4, AO2 5. Level 3 needs secure knowledge of the concept applied to the figures and a clear argument.
Common trap: Misunderstanding the term, or only describing the resource without knowledge of the concept.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: Evaluate the success of one urban pollution reduction policy. (9 marks)
back:
Model answer: London's ULEZ (2019, London-wide from 2023) charges older polluting vehicles. Roadside nitrogen dioxide fell in the zone, according to the Mayor of London's reports. Limits: cost to low-income drivers, and particulates from tyres and brakes remain. Compare with odd-even driving schemes in Delhi. Judgement: partly successful.
Marking points: AO1 4, AO2 5. Level 3 needs evidence of outcomes and a supported evaluation.
Common trap: Describing the policy without judging success, or giving no example to support the evaluation.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: To what extent does recycling urban waste reduce pressure on the carbon cycle? (9 marks)
back:
Model answer: Recycling cuts the need for raw materials and energy, so fewer fossil carbon stores are released. It avoids landfill, where waste decomposes slowly and releases methane over decades. Transport and exporting waste add emissions. Incineration releases carbon quickly but can recover energy. Judgement on the extent.
Marking points: AO1 4, AO2 5. This is a synoptic link to Water and carbon. Level 3 uses carbon cycle concepts.
Common trap: Broad "global warming" links with no stores, sinks, flows or fast and slow cycle ideas.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: Assess the success of a river restoration project in a damaged urban catchment. (9 marks)
back:
Model answer: The River Quaggy at Sutcliffe Park, London, was restored around 2004. Aims: flood storage and habitat. Parties: the Environment Agency, the council and local groups. Activities: the culvert was removed and the channel re-meandered over a floodplain park. Outcomes: flood storage, wildlife and public access, but it is a small scale. Judgement.
Marking points: AO1 4, AO2 5. Credit the reasons, aims, parties, activities and evaluated outcomes.
Common trap: A generic account of restoration with no named project or evaluation of its outcomes.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: To what extent does urban regeneration change the meaning of a place for its existing residents? (9 marks)
back:
Model answer: Regeneration rebrands places for outsiders. Stratford's Olympic Park gave new meaning to investors and visitors. Long-term residents can feel priced out and that their place has been taken. Some gain jobs and pride. Judgement: meaning changes more for outsiders than for existing insiders.
Marking points: AO1 4, AO2 5. This links Changing places with urban option content. Level 3 needs examples and a clear view.
Common trap: Describing the regeneration scheme without addressing place meaning or residents.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: Assess the extent to which strategies to manage economic inequality in a contrasting urban area have been successful. (20 marks)
back:
Model answer: In Mumbai, Dharavi's informal economy sits beside wealthy districts. Strategies: slum rehabilitation, upgrading and the Dharavi redevelopment tender won by the Adani Group in 2022. Evaluate who gains, the risk of displacement and the slow progress. Compare with London policies if useful. Conclusion.
Marking points: AO1 10, AO2 10. Level 4 needs detailed place knowledge and evaluation.
Common trap: Contrasting places that cannot be compared, such as a megacity and a village, or a long history instead of an argument.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: 'Sustainable cities are more of a goal than a reality.' To what extent do you agree? (20 marks)
back:
Model answer: Define the natural, physical, social and economic dimensions. Curitiba's bus rapid transit and Freiburg's Vauban show real progress. Masdar's completion date has slipped repeatedly. Most cities improve one dimension while others lag. Conclusion: a clear judgement.
Marking points: AO1 10, AO2 10. Level 4 needs the concept defined and examples evaluated against it.
Common trap: No clear definition of sustainability, or listing eco-projects without judging how sustainable each city is.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 2: Human geography

front: Which word set describes Level 4 work in the AQA Geography NEA levels?
back: Detailed, effective, thorough, complete, well-developed
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 3: Geographical investigation (NEA)

front: Which word set describes Level 2 work in the AQA Geography NEA levels?
back: Intermittent, partial, some, implicit, imprecise, inconsistent
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 3: Geographical investigation (NEA)

front: How do you write an NEA title and introduction that reaches Level 4 in Area 1?
back:
Model answer: A focused, testable question with a theoretical basis and a named location, such as "To what extent does pebble size decrease in the direction of longshore drift at a named beach?". Link it to the spec (coastal transport). Review literature and theory, and compare with other studies.
Marking points: Area 1, 10 marks AO3. Level 4 (9-10): question effectively identified and completely referenced to the spec; theoretical and comparative contexts well understood and stated.
Common trap: A broad, generalised title, or a literature section that is never linked to the question.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 3: Geographical investigation (NEA)

front: How do you write the methods section of an NEA to reach Level 4 in Area 2?
back:
Model answer: Describe each method, with its sampling (systematic every 50 m along a transect, stratified by land use), sample size, frequency and timing. Justify each choice: why it is representative, accurate and safe, and how it answers the aim. Mention a pilot study and the risks.
Marking points: Area 2, 15 marks AO3. Level 4 (12-15): detailed range of approaches including sampling, thorough and well-reasoned justification, detailed implementation.
Common trap: Describing what you did without justifying why, which is "some justification" (Level 2).
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 3: Geographical investigation (NEA)

front: How do you reach Level 4 in Area 3 (Methods of critical analysis) of the NEA?
back:
Model answer: Choose techniques that suit the data, such as Spearman's rank for a relationship or chi-squared for a distribution, with a significance level. Interpret the results against theory and expected patterns. Comment on accuracy, representativeness and anomalies, and say what the fieldwork taught you.
Marking points: Area 3, 20 marks (AO2 6, AO3 14). Level 4 (15-20): effective techniques, thorough critical examination of data, effective use of theory to order observations.
Common trap: Presenting many graphs with only description, never interrogating the data or linking to theory.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 3: Geographical investigation (NEA)

front: In an NEA, 6 sites give a Spearman's rank sum of d squared of 8. Calculate rs and say how to judge whether it is significant.
back:
Model answer: rs = 1 - (6 x 8) / (6^3 - 6) = 1 - 48/210 = 1 - 0.229 = 0.77. This is a strong positive correlation. Compare 0.77 with the critical value for n = 6 at the 0.05 significance level in a table.
Marking points: Correct formula, correct working, the direction and strength, then a significance test against critical values.
Common trap: Using n squared instead of n cubed minus n, or stating a strong correlation as proof without testing significance.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 3: Geographical investigation (NEA)

front: How do you write NEA conclusions and evaluation that reach Level 4 in Area 4?
back:
Model answer: Summarise the results for each aim, then answer the title with a well-argued case. Relate the findings to the wider context and theory. Evaluate the methods, accuracy and limitations, the ethical dimensions and ideas for further research.
Marking points: Area 4, 15 marks AO3. Level 4 (12-15): thorough, logical write-up with a range of presentation methods, effective evaluation, complete link to wider context, thorough ethics.
Common trap: A conclusion that repeats the results without answering the question, or leaving out ethics.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 3: Geographical investigation (NEA)

front: How should ethics appear in an AQA Geography NEA?
back:
Model answer: Explain the consent and anonymity of questionnaire respondents, permission to use private land, avoiding damage to sites, and fair representation of communities in how data is presented.
Marking points: Area 4, AO3: Level 4 needs a thorough understanding of the ethical dimensions of field research.
Common trap: A single line on safety (a risk assessment) mistaken for ethics.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 3: Geographical investigation (NEA)

front: How should data be presented in an NEA to score well in Area 4?
back:
Model answer: Use a range of methods suited to each data type, such as located proportional symbols on maps, scatter graphs with best-fit lines and annotated photos. Each one is titled, labelled, scaled and referred to in the text.
Marking points: Area 4 (AO3 strand 3): Level 4 needs a thorough, clear and logical write-up using a range of presentation methods.
Common trap: Many similar bar charts or decorative graphs that are never analysed in the text.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Exam technique::Paper 3: Geographical investigation (NEA)
